# The Byzantine Empire: A History of Rome’s Eastern Continuation  
### Prepared by Alice for John Smith

The Byzantine Empire was, in its own eyes, not Byzantine at all. Its inhabitants called themselves Romans, their emperor was the Roman emperor, and their capital—Constantinople—was the New Rome. The term “Byzantine” was coined centuries later by Western scholars, deriving from Byzantion, the ancient Greek settlement upon which Constantinople was built. Yet the name has endured because it captures something distinctive: a Christian, Greek-speaking, eastern Mediterranean civilization that preserved Roman political traditions while transforming them through Christianity, Greek culture, and centuries of interaction with neighboring peoples.

Its history lasted for more than a millennium. From the foundation of Constantinople in the fourth century to the city’s fall to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, the empire experienced extraordinary renewal and catastrophic decline. It survived invasions, religious disputes, civil wars, economic crises, and the rise of rival powers. It produced monumental architecture, sophisticated law, illuminated manuscripts, theological controversies, military innovations, and a diplomatic culture of remarkable subtlety. It also witnessed the gradual contraction of Roman power from a Mediterranean empire into a resilient state centered on Constantinople and its surrounding territories.

## The Roman Origins of Constantinople

The Byzantine story began within the Roman Empire. By the third century, Rome’s vast territories had become increasingly difficult to govern from a single center. Emperors spent more time near vulnerable frontiers, especially along the Rhine, Danube, and eastern borders. The empire’s political geography was changing, and the eastern provinces—wealthier, more urbanized, and more densely populated than many western regions—were becoming increasingly important.

In 284, the emperor Diocletian reorganized imperial administration. He divided the empire into multiple administrative units and introduced the Tetrarchy, a system in which two senior emperors and two junior colleagues governed different regions. Although this arrangement did not permanently divide the empire, it established a pattern of shared rule and encouraged emperors to establish courts closer to the frontiers.

A decisive transformation came under Constantine the Great. After defeating his rival Licinius in 324, Constantine became sole ruler of the Roman world. He selected Byzantion, an ancient Greek city located on a strategically vital peninsula between Europe and Asia, as the site of a new imperial capital. Dedicated in 330, Constantinople commanded the Bosporus, linking the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Its position offered commercial advantages and allowed the emperor to monitor the Danube frontier, the eastern provinces, and maritime routes.

Constantine’s reign also transformed the religious character of the empire. His conversion to Christianity and his patronage of the Christian church did not immediately make Christianity the sole imperial religion, but they altered the relationship between state and faith. Constantine sponsored churches, supported Christian institutions, and convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 to address theological disputes concerning the nature of Christ. The Nicene formulation would become central to imperial Christianity, although theological conflict continued for centuries.

Constantinople was designed to rival Rome. It possessed a monumental forum, an imperial palace, public baths, churches, and a ceremonial avenue. Its location on a peninsula made it defensible, and its walls were repeatedly strengthened. The city’s natural harbor, the Golden Horn, supported trade and naval activity. Over time, Constantinople became not merely an administrative center but the symbolic heart of the eastern Roman world.

## The Division of the Roman Empire

After Constantine’s death in 337, the empire continued to be governed by members of his dynasty, but internal rivalry and external pressure remained persistent. The Roman world was never neatly divided into two entirely separate states. Emperors continued to claim authority over the whole empire, and the eastern and western halves remained connected through law, military structures, commerce, and dynastic politics.

Nevertheless, administrative separation became more pronounced. In 395, after the death of Theodosius I, the empire was again divided between his sons: Arcadius governed the East and Honorius the West. This division proved enduring in practice. The eastern empire was wealthier, more urbanized, and better able to sustain taxation and military administration. The western empire faced severe pressures from Germanic migrations, civil conflict, fiscal weakness, and the loss of territories.

The sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 shocked the Roman world. Rome remained symbolically important, but it was no longer the secure center of imperial power. In 476, the Germanic military leader Odoacer deposed the western emperor Romulus Augustulus. Traditionally, this event is treated as the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Yet the eastern emperor in Constantinople did not regard the Roman Empire as having ended. From the eastern perspective, there was still one Roman emperor, and the western territories had simply fallen under the rule of local kings and military leaders.

The eastern empire inherited Roman institutions and law, but it also developed its own character. Greek was widely spoken in the eastern provinces and eventually became the dominant language of government and culture, though Latin remained important in administration and legal tradition for centuries. Christianity provided a shared ideological framework, while the eastern Mediterranean’s cities, trade networks, and intellectual traditions sustained a vibrant urban civilization.

## Justinian and the Ambition to Restore Rome

The sixth century opened with the reign of Justinian I, one of the most consequential emperors in Roman and Byzantine history. Justinian came to power in 527 and ruled until 565. His reign combined legal reform, military reconquest, architectural magnificence, religious controversy, and political upheaval.

Justinian’s greatest legal achievement was the compilation of Roman law. Under the direction of the jurist Tribonian, imperial legislation and earlier legal writings were organized into what later generations called the Corpus Juris Civilis, or Body of Civil Law. It included the Codex, containing imperial laws; the Digest, drawn from the writings of earlier jurists; the Institutes, a textbook for legal students; and later legislation known as the Novellae. Although the compilation did not instantly replace every local legal practice, it became one of the most influential legal works in European history. Centuries later, it would shape the legal systems of much of continental Europe.

Justinian also pursued the reconquest of former western Roman territories. The general Belisarius invaded the Vandal kingdom in North Africa in 533. The campaign succeeded with surprising speed, restoring imperial control over Carthage and much of the former Vandal realm. Belisarius then turned toward Italy, where the Ostrogothic kingdom had ruled since the late fifth century. The Gothic War, beginning in 535, lasted for decades and devastated the Italian peninsula. Rome changed hands repeatedly, cities were besieged, and agricultural production suffered. By the early 550s, imperial forces had defeated the Ostrogoths, and Italy was nominally restored to Roman rule.

The empire also recovered parts of southeastern Spain from the Visigoths. Justinian’s ambition was not merely territorial. He aimed to restore the Roman imperial order around the Mediterranean. Yet reconquest was expensive, and the restored territories were vulnerable. The Lombards invaded Italy soon after Justinian’s death, limiting imperial control largely to coastal and southern regions.

Justinian’s reign is also remembered for the construction of Hagia Sophia. The previous church on the site had been destroyed during the Nika revolt of 532, a violent uprising that nearly toppled the emperor. Justinian commissioned the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus to create a vast new church. Completed in 537, Hagia Sophia’s enormous dome seemed to float above the interior, supported by an innovative system of arches and pendentives. It became the most celebrated monument of Constantinople and a symbol of imperial Christianity.

The Nika revolt revealed the volatility of urban politics. Chariot-racing factions, often associated with the Blues and Greens, had social and political significance beyond sport. Their supporters could mobilize large crowds, and tensions over taxation, legal disputes, and imperial administration contributed to the uprising. Justinian initially considered fleeing, but Empress Theodora reportedly urged him to remain and confront the crisis. The revolt was suppressed with great violence, and the rebuilding of Constantinople transformed the city.

Theodora herself was an influential political partner. She supported religious positions associated with non-Chalcedonian Christians and advocated measures affecting women’s legal and social status. Though the surviving sources reflect the prejudices of their authors, her role demonstrates that imperial power was not exercised by emperors alone.

Justinian’s policies imposed significant burdens. His wars, construction projects, and administrative apparatus required heavy taxation. The empire was also struck by plague beginning in 541, probably part of the first major pandemic historically associated with bubonic plague. The disease affected Constantinople and many other regions, reducing populations and weakening economic and military capacity. By the end of Justinian’s reign, the empire remained formidable but was strained by the cost of universal ambition.

## Crisis and Survival in the Seventh Century

The decades after Justinian were marked by instability. The empire confronted the Avars and Slavs in the Balkans, the Persian Sasanian Empire in the east, and internal political conflict. Under Emperor Heraclius, who came to power in 610, the Persian war reached an extraordinary level of intensity.

The Sasanian ruler Khosrow II seized Byzantine territories in Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and Anatolia. Persian forces captured Jerusalem in 614 and took the relic believed to be the True Cross. Egypt, a crucial source of grain and tax revenue, was lost. Constantinople itself appeared threatened.

Heraclius reorganized imperial finances and military operations. From 622 onward, he conducted a series of campaigns that shifted the balance. Byzantine forces invaded Persian territory, and in 627 defeated the Persians near Nineveh. Internal conflict within the Sasanian state led to Khosrow’s overthrow and a peace settlement. Byzantine rule was restored in much of the lost territory, but the victory was short-lived.

Within a few years, Arab armies emerging from the Arabian Peninsula conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and much of the eastern provinces. These conquests were driven by a combination of religious, political, and military factors. The Byzantine and Persian empires had exhausted one another in their long war, leaving both vulnerable. By the 640s, the eastern Mediterranean political order had been fundamentally transformed.

The loss of Egypt and Syria was a watershed. These provinces had been among the richest and most urbanized parts of the Roman world. Their loss reduced the empire’s tax base and changed its strategic priorities. The empire increasingly centered on Anatolia, Thrace, the Aegean, and Constantinople. The old Mediterranean empire became a more compact and militarized state.

Constantinople survived repeated Arab sieges, especially in 674–678 and 717–718. The city’s fortifications, naval power, and defensive technologies were crucial. Greek fire, a combustible substance used in naval warfare, was particularly feared, though its precise composition remains unknown. The survival of Constantinople prevented the eastern Roman state from suffering the fate of many neighboring powers and preserved a Christian imperial center for centuries.

The seventh century also saw profound administrative changes. The empire’s military provinces, often called themes, developed as a response to the new strategic environment. Armies were settled in regions where they could defend local territory, and military and civil administration became more closely connected. The precise origins and development of the theme system remain debated, but it helped the empire mobilize resources in a period of contraction.

The language and identity of the empire changed as well. Latin receded, while Greek became increasingly dominant in administration and public culture. Yet the rulers and inhabitants continued to identify themselves as Romans. “Roman” became a political and religious identity rather than simply a reflection of Latin language or control over the ancient city of Rome.

## Iconoclasm and the Transformation of Imperial Christianity

One of the most divisive episodes in Byzantine history was the controversy over religious images, known as Iconoclasm. Beginning in the eighth century and recurring into the ninth, emperors and churchmen argued over whether icons—painted or sculpted representations of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the saints—were legitimate objects of devotion or a form of idolatry.

Emperor Leo III initiated policies against images in the 720s, though the exact sequence and extent of early iconoclastic measures remain debated. His son Constantine V strongly supported the movement and convened the Council of Hieria in 754, which rejected the veneration of icons. Iconoclast emperors argued that divine nature could not be represented and that the use of images blurred the distinction between Creator and creation.

Since God had become human in Christ, they argued, the visible representation of Christ was possible and the veneration shown to an image could pass to the person represented. The theologian John of Damascus, writing under Muslim rule, became one of the most influential defenders of images.

Monks were among the strongest defenders of icons, and iconoclast policies sometimes targeted monastic property and influence. The debate also affected relations with the papacy, which generally favored the veneration of images.

The controversy left a lasting mark on Byzantine theology, art, and the relationship between imperial power and the church.

## The Macedonian Renaissance

The ninth through eleventh centuries witnessed a major revival of Byzantine political power and cultural production. This era is often associated with the Macedonian dynasty, which ruled from 867 to 1056, though the term “Macedonian Renaissance” refers more broadly to intellectual and artistic renewal.

Byzantine scholars collected, copied, and commented on ancient Greek texts. Classical literature, philosophy, medicine, and science were preserved in manuscript traditions that later became crucial to the transmission of Greek learning. This was not simple imitation of antiquity. Byzantine intellectuals interpreted classical works through Christian frameworks and applied them to contemporary education, theology, and administration.

The empire’s foreign relations also expanded. Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius developed a written script and translated Christian texts for Slavic peoples. Their mission to Moravia had lasting effects, and their disciples helped spread Christianity and literacy among the Bulgarians and other Slavic communities. The script associated with their tradition, Cyrillic, became central to the written cultures of several eastern European societies.

The conversion of Bulgaria to Christianity in the ninth century was a major achievement, though relations between Byzantium and Bulgaria were often marked by warfare. The Bulgarian ruler Simeon I sought recognition as emperor and challenged Constantinople militarily and diplomatically. The conflict ended only after prolonged struggle.

Basil is remembered in later tradition as the “Bulgar-Slayer,” a title reflecting his campaigns against the Bulgarian Empire. Byzantine forces defeated Bulgaria after decades of war, and the region was incorporated into the imperial sphere. Basil also strengthened control in Armenia and expanded influence in the Caucasus.

The military and administrative structures of the middle Byzantine period were sophisticated. Provincial commanders, aristocratic landowners, and military families competed for influence. The state sought to preserve the tax base and prevent powerful magnates from absorbing the land of small farmers. Laws attempted to limit the concentration of land, though enforcement varied.

The imperial court in Constantinople became a center of ceremonial, diplomacy, and political theater. Foreign ambassadors were impressed—or intimidated—by elaborate rituals designed to present the emperor as the earthly representative of divine order. Relations between the Byzantine church and the Latin church had long been marked by differences in language, liturgy, ecclesiastical organization, and political culture. These tensions eventually contributed to the schism traditionally dated to 1054.

The dispute involved papal authority, the jurisdiction of the patriarch of Constantinople, liturgical customs, and theological differences such as the Filioque controversy. Western Christians increasingly included the phrase “and the Son” in the creed’s statement about the procession of the Holy Spirit. Byzantine theologians objected both to the theological formulation and to the unilateral alteration of the creed.

In 1054, representatives of Pope Leo IX and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchanged excommunications. The event was not immediately understood as an irreversible division across all Christian communities, and communication continued afterward. Yet it came to symbolize the growing separation between Roman Catholicism in the West and Eastern Orthodoxy in the Byzantine world.

After Basil II’s death, the empire faced growing political instability. Civil wars, succession disputes, fiscal problems, and pressure from external enemies weakened central authority. The arrival of the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia created a new and formidable challenge.

At the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was defeated and captured by the Seljuk ruler Alp Arslan. The emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who came to power in 1081, stabilized the state through a combination of military reform, diplomacy, and fiscal measures. He faced Normans in the Balkans, Pechenegs north of the Danube, and Turkish powers in Anatolia. Alexios appealed to the papacy and western rulers for military assistance, contributing to the launching of the First Crusade.

Latin leaders established their own principalities in the Levant, and Byzantine-western relations deteriorated.

The Komnenian emperors maintained a reduced but influential empire. Alexios, John II, and Manuel I strengthened the army, cultivated aristocratic networks, and projected power into the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. Manuel I in particular pursued an ambitious foreign policy involving Hungary, Italy, the Crusader states, and the Muslim powers of the Near East.

The Empire of Nicaea eventually emerged as the strongest successor state. Its rulers preserved imperial institutions, supported the Orthodox church, and gradually recovered territory. In 1261, Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured Constantinople and restored Byzantine rule.

The empire that returned to Constantinople was greatly diminished. The city’s population had fallen, its economy was damaged, and much of the former imperial territory was controlled by rival states. The restored empire had to contend with Venice, Genoa, western principalities, Balkan rulers, and Turkish powers.

## The Palaiologan Era

The Palaiologan dynasty ruled from 1259 until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its reign was characterized by cultural brilliance, political fragmentation, military weakness, and eventual Ottoman conquest.

Michael VIII Palaiologos sought to secure the restored empire diplomatically. At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, he accepted a form of church union with Rome in hopes of preventing a western attack. The agreement faced strong opposition among Byzantine clergy and population. Many Byzantines believed that doctrinal compromise threatened Orthodox identity, while the promised military assistance was limited.

The union failed to produce lasting security. Byzantine resources were stretched by conflicts in the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Mediterranean. Genoa and Venice competed for commercial privileges, and the empire increasingly relied on foreign powers whose interests did not align with Constantinople’s.

Under Andronikos II, the empire’s military capacity declined. The reduction of the navy and reliance on mercenaries weakened defenses. In Anatolia, Turkish principalities expanded rapidly. Among them was the Ottoman polity, founded by Osman in the late thirteenth century. The Ottomans initially controlled territory in northwestern Anatolia but soon crossed into Europe and established themselves in the Balkans.

The fourteenth century brought civil wars, financial crises, plague, and territorial losses. The empire became a patchwork of Constantinople, parts of the Peloponnese, Thessaloniki at various times, and scattered holdings. The Ottoman advance was relentless, though Byzantine diplomacy sometimes exploited rivalries among Ottoman princes and neighboring states.

The Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347 was especially destructive. Competing factions supported different candidates for the throne, and foreign powers intervened. The conflict weakened the state and enabled Ottoman expansion. The empire’s remaining resources were further diminished by the Black Death, which reached Constantinople and other regions in the mid-fourteenth century.

Despite political decline, the Palaiologan period was a time of remarkable intellectual and artistic achievement. Byzantine scholars studied ancient philosophy and science, and some later traveled to Italy, contributing to the Renaissance’s renewed interest in Greek learning. Manuscript production continued, as did theological debate and artistic innovation.

The hesychast controversy, associated with Gregory Palamas, concerned the nature of mystical prayer and the possibility of experiencing divine grace. Palamas distinguished between God’s inaccessible essence and the divine energies through which God could be experienced. The controversy reflected the continuing vitality of Byzantine theology even amid political crisis.

The empire’s cultural influence extended beyond its borders. Orthodox Christianity shaped the religious and political traditions of Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, and other eastern European societies. # The Byzantine Empire: A History of Rome’s Eastern Continuation  
### Prepared by Alice for John Smith

Its history lasted for more than a millennium. From the foundation of Constantinople in the fourth century to the city’s fall to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, the empire experienced extraordinary renewal and catastrophic decline. It survived invasions, religious disputes, civil wars, economic crises, and the rise of rival powers. It produced monumental architecture, sophisticated law, illuminated manuscripts, theological controversies, military innovations, and a diplomatic culture of remarkable subtlety. It also witnessed the gradual contraction of Roman power from a Mediterranean empire into a resilient state centered on Constantinople and its surrounding territories.

Emperors spent more time near vulnerable frontiers, especially along the Rhine, Danube, and eastern borders. The empire’s political geography was changing, and the eastern provinces—wealthier, more urbanized, and more densely populated than many western regions—were becoming increasingly important.

In 284, the emperor Diocletian reorganized imperial administration. He divided the empire into multiple administrative units and introduced the Tetrarchy, a system in which two senior emperors and two junior colleagues governed different regions. Although this arrangement did not permanently divide the empire, it established a pattern of shared rule and encouraged emperors to establish courts closer to the frontiers.

A decisive transformation came under Constantine the Great. After defeating his rival Licinius in 324, Constantine became sole ruler of the Roman world. He selected Byzantion, an ancient Greek city located on a strategically vital peninsula between Europe and Asia, as the site of a new imperial capital. Dedicated in 330, Constantinople commanded the Bosporus, linking the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Its position offered commercial advantages and allowed the emperor to monitor the Danube frontier, the eastern provinces, and maritime routes.

Constantine’s reign also transformed the religious character of the empire. His conversion to Christianity and his patronage of the Christian church did not immediately make Christianity the sole imperial religion, but they altered the relationship between state and faith. Constantine sponsored churches, supported Christian institutions, and convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 to address theological disputes concerning the nature of Christ. The Nicene formulation would become central to imperial Christianity, although theological conflict continued for centuries.

Constantinople was designed to rival Rome. It possessed a monumental forum, an imperial palace, public baths, churches, and a ceremonial avenue. Its location on a peninsula made it defensible, and its walls were repeatedly strengthened. The city’s natural harbor, the Golden Horn, supported trade and naval activity. Over time, Constantinople became not merely an administrative center but the symbolic heart of the eastern Roman world.

## The Division of the Roman Empire

After Constantine’s death in 337, the empire continued to be governed by members of his dynasty, but internal rivalry and external pressure remained persistent. The Roman world was never neatly divided into two entirely separate states. Emperors continued to claim authority over the whole empire, and the eastern and western halves remained connected through law, military structures, commerce, and dynastic politics.

Nevertheless, administrative separation became more pronounced. In 395, after the death of Theodosius I, the empire was again divided between his sons: Arcadius governed the East and Honorius the West. This division proved enduring in practice. The eastern empire was wealthier, more urbanized, and better able to sustain taxation and military administration. The western empire faced severe pressures from Germanic migrations, civil conflict, fiscal weakness, and the loss of territories.

The sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 shocked the Roman world. Rome remained symbolically important, but it was no longer the secure center of imperial power. Yet the eastern emperor in Constantinople did not regard the Roman Empire as having ended. From the eastern perspective, there was still one Roman emperor, and the western territories had simply fallen under the rule of local kings and military leaders.

The eastern empire inherited Roman institutions and law, but it also developed its own character. But the subsequent political disorder enabled Turkish forces to establish themselves across much of Anatolia, the empire’s principal recruiting ground and economic heartland.

Anatolia had been central to Byzantine survival since the seventh century. Its loss reduced manpower, tax revenue, and agricultural production. The empire’s military system was increasingly dependent on foreign mercenaries, and provincial elites gained leverage over imperial politics.

The emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who came to power in 1081, stabilized the state through a combination of military reform, diplomacy, and fiscal measures. He faced Normans in the Balkans, Pechenegs north of the Danube, and Turkish powers in Anatolia. Alexios appealed to the papacy and western rulers for military assistance, contributing to the launching of the First Crusade.

The crusading movement created both opportunity and danger. Western armies passed through Byzantine territory, and Alexios hoped they would help recover lands lost to the Turks. He sought oaths from crusader leaders promising to return former imperial territories. Some cooperation occurred, and Nicaea was restored to Byzantine control. But mutual distrust soon grew. Latin leaders established their own principalities in the Levant, and Byzantine-western relations deteriorated.

The Komnenian emperors maintained a reduced but influential empire. Alexios, John II, and Manuel I strengthened the army, cultivated aristocratic networks, and projected power into the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. Manuel I in particular pursued an ambitious foreign policy involving Hungary, Italy, the Crusader states, and the Muslim powers of the Near East.

Yet the restoration was fragile. The empire’s dependence on aristocratic families and foreign military forces created structural weaknesses. Commercial privileges granted to Italian maritime republics brought short-term benefits but gradually undermined Byzantine control of trade.

## The Fourth Crusade and the Sack of Constantinople

The catastrophe of 1204 was one of the most consequential events in Byzantine history. The Fourth Crusade, initially intended to attack Muslim Egypt, became entangled in Venetian financial interests and Byzantine dynastic politics.

The crusaders agreed to assist the deposed Byzantine prince Alexios Angelos, who promised money, military support, and church union in exchange for help restoring his father to the throne. After entering Constantinople in 1203, the crusaders restored Isaac II and Alexios IV. Their promises proved impossible to fulfill, and resentment between the local population and the western forces intensified.

In April 1204, crusader armies captured and sacked Constantinople. Churches, palaces, libraries, and private homes were looted. The violence shocked contemporaries, including some western Christian observers. The Hagia Sophia was desecrated, relics were carried away, and the city’s wealth was dispersed across Europe.

The crusaders established the Latin Empire of Constantinople. Byzantine territories were divided among Latin rulers, Venetian interests, and local Greek successor states. The principal Byzantine centers of resistance were the Empire of Nicaea in western Anatolia, the Despotate of Epirus in the Balkans, and the Empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea coast.

The Empire of Nicaea eventually emerged as the strongest successor state. Its rulers preserved imperial institutions, supported the Orthodox church, and gradually recovered territory. In 1261, Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured Constantinople and restored Byzantine rule.

The empire that returned to Constantinople was greatly diminished. The city’s population had fallen, its economy was damaged, and much of the former imperial territory was controlled by rival states. The restored empire had to contend with Venice, Genoa, western principalities, Balkan rulers, and Turkish powers.

The sack of 1204 permanently damaged relations between Byzantium and the Latin West. Although negotiations over church union continued, many Byzantines regarded western military and religious ambitions as more dangerous than any temporary alliance might be useful.

## The Palaiologan Era

The Palaiologan dynasty ruled from 1259 until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its reign was characterized by cultural brilliance, political fragmentation, military weakness, and eventual Ottoman conquest.

Michael VIII Palaiologos sought to secure the restored empire diplomatically. At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, he accepted a form of church union with Rome in hopes of preventing a western attack. The agreement faced strong opposition among Byzantine clergy and population. Many Byzantines believed that doctrinal compromise threatened Orthodox identity, while the promised military assistance was limited.

The union failed to produce lasting security. Byzantine resources were stretched by conflicts in the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Mediterranean. Genoa and Venice competed for commercial privileges, and the empire increasingly relied on foreign powers whose interests did not align with Constantinople’s.

Under Andronikos II, the empire’s military capacity declined. The reduction of the navy and reliance on mercenaries weakened defenses. In Anatolia, Turkish principalities expanded rapidly. Among them was the Ottoman polity, founded by Osman in the late thirteenth century. The Ottomans initially controlled territory in northwestern Anatolia but soon crossed into Europe and established themselves in the Balkans.

The fourteenth century brought civil wars, financial crises, plague, and territorial losses. The empire became a patchwork of Constantinople, parts of the Peloponnese, Thessaloniki at various times, and scattered holdings. The Ottoman advance was relentless, though Byzantine diplomacy sometimes exploited rivalries among Ottoman princes and neighboring states.

The Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347 was especially destructive. Competing factions supported different candidates for the throne, and foreign powers intervened. The conflict weakened the state and enabled Ottoman expansion. The empire’s remaining resources were further diminished by the Black Death, which reached Constantinople and other regions in the mid-fourteenth century.

Despite political decline, the Palaiologan period was a time of remarkable intellectual and artistic achievement. Byzantine scholars studied ancient philosophy and science, and some later traveled to Italy, contributing to the Renaissance’s renewed interest in Greek learning. Manuscript production continued, as did theological debate and artistic innovation.

The hesychast controversy, associated with Gregory Palamas, concerned the nature of mystical prayer and the possibility of experiencing divine grace. Palamas distinguished between God’s inaccessible essence and the divine energies through which God could be experienced. The controversy reflected the continuing vitality of Byzantine theology even amid political crisis.

The empire’s cultural influence extended beyond its borders. Orthodox Christianity shaped the religious and political traditions of Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, and other eastern European societies. Byzantine artistic forms, liturgical practices, legal ideas, and models of rulership continued to influence neighboring civilizations long after imperial territory had contracted.

## The Final Struggle

By the fifteenth century, Constantinople was largely surrounded by Ottoman lands. The city remained symbolically powerful and possessed formidable walls, but its population and economic base had greatly declined. The Byzantine emperors appealed repeatedly to western Europe for assistance, often linking aid to church union.

Emperor John VIII Palaiologos attended the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438–1439. A union between the Greek and Latin churches was proclaimed, but it was unpopular among many Byzantines and did not generate sufficient military support. The slogan that it was better to see the Turkish turban in Constantinople than the Latin mitre captured the depth of opposition to western ecclesiastical control, though its exact historical context is debated.

In 1451, Mehmed II became Ottoman sultan. He was determined to capture Constantinople and transform it into the center of a new imperial order. He constructed the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the European shore of the Bosporus, strengthened Ottoman artillery, and assembled a large army.

The siege began in April 1453. Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos commanded a small defending force composed of Byzantines, Genoese, Venetians, and other volunteers. The city’s walls remained formidable, but the defenders were vastly outnumbered. Ottoman cannon battered the fortifications, while ships attempted to blockade the harbor. Mehmed famously transported ships overland into the Golden Horn to bypass the defensive chain.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottomans launched their final assault. Constantine XI disappeared in the fighting and was remembered as a heroic final emperor. Constantinople fell, ending the Byzantine Empire after more than a thousand years of imperial history.

The conquest was not the end of the city. Mehmed II made Constantinople—soon increasingly called Istanbul—the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The city was repopulated and rebuilt, while Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque. Byzantine administrative, artistic, and intellectual traditions continued within the Ottoman world.

## Legacy

The Byzantine Empire’s legacy is vast and complex. It preserved Roman law, statecraft, Christianity, and Greek learning through centuries when political structures in the western Mediterranean were transformed. Its scholars copied ancient texts that might otherwise have been lost. Its theologians shaped Eastern Orthodox Christianity. Its artists developed the icon, mosaic, manuscript illumination, and architectural traditions that influenced regions from the Balkans to Russia.

Its political culture also left a deep imprint. The Byzantine emperor was portrayed as God’s chosen ruler and guardian of Christian order, though emperors were frequently challenged, deposed, or killed. The empire’s diplomacy anticipated forms of international politics based on ceremonial status, dynastic marriage, intelligence, subsidies, and indirect influence.

Byzantium’s history also demonstrates the adaptability of imperial systems. It survived the collapse of the western Roman world, the rise of Islam, the loss of major provinces, religious civil conflict, and the devastation of 1204. It repeatedly reorganized its institutions and redefined its identity while maintaining a continuous claim to Roman legitimacy.

At the same time, its decline was not caused by a single weakness. It resulted from overlapping pressures: shrinking territory, fiscal strain, aristocratic rivalry, military dependence, commercial concessions, epidemic disease, civil war, and the rise of powerful external states. The Fourth Crusade inflicted a wound from which the empire never fully recovered, while the Ottoman conquest completed a transformation already underway.

To study Byzantium is therefore to study continuity amid change. The empire was Roman in its political memory, Greek in much of its language and culture, Christian in its worldview, and profoundly shaped by the peoples and powers around it. Its thousand-year history cannot be reduced either to a fading remnant of Rome or to a separate civilization disconnected from antiquity. It was a living, evolving society that carried the Roman imperial tradition into the medieval world—and whose influence remains visible in law, religion, art, architecture, literature, and political thought today.

# The Byzantine Empire: A History of Rome’s Eastern Continuation  
### Prepared by Alice for John Smith

The Byzantine Empire was, in its own eyes, not Byzantine at all. Its inhabitants called themselves Romans, their emperor was the Roman emperor, and their capital—Constantinople—was the New Rome. The term “Byzantine” was coined centuries later by Western scholars, deriving from Byzantion, the ancient Greek settlement upon which Constantinople was built. Yet the name has endured because it captures something distinctive: a Christian, Greek-speaking, eastern Mediterranean civilization that preserved Roman political traditions while transforming them through Christianity, Greek culture, and centuries of interaction with neighboring peoples.

Its history lasted for more than a millennium. From the foundation of Constantinople in the fourth century to the city’s fall to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, the empire experienced extraordinary renewal and catastrophic decline. It survived invasions, religious disputes, civil wars, economic crises, and the rise of rival powers. It produced monumental architecture, sophisticated law, illuminated manuscripts, theological controversies, military innovations, and a diplomatic culture of remarkable subtlety. It also witnessed the gradual contraction of Roman power from a Mediterranean empire into a resilient state centered on Constantinople and its surrounding territories.

## The Roman Origins of Constantinople

The Byzantine story began within the Roman Empire. By the third century, Rome’s vast territories had become increasingly difficult to govern from a single center. Emperors spent more time near vulnerable frontiers, especially along the Rhine, Danube, and eastern borders. The empire’s political geography was changing, and the eastern provinces—wealthier, more urbanized, and more densely populated than many western regions—were becoming increasingly important.

In 284, the emperor Diocletian reorganized imperial administration. He divided the empire into multiple administrative units and introduced the Tetrarchy, a system in which two senior emperors and two junior colleagues governed different regions. Although this arrangement did not permanently divide the empire, it established a pattern of shared rule and encouraged emperors to establish courts closer to the frontiers.

A decisive transformation came under Constantine the Great. After defeating his rival Licinius in 324, Constantine became sole ruler of the Roman world. He selected Byzantion, an ancient Greek city located on a strategically vital peninsula between Europe and Asia, as the site of a new imperial capital. Dedicated in 330, Constantinople commanded the Bosporus, linking the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Its position offered commercial advantages and allowed the emperor to monitor the Danube frontier, the eastern provinces, and maritime routes.

Constantine’s reign also transformed the religious character of the empire. His conversion to Christianity and his patronage of the Christian church did not immediately make Christianity the sole imperial religion, but they altered the relationship between state and faith. Constantine sponsored churches, supported Christian institutions, and convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 to address theological disputes concerning the nature of Christ. The Nicene formulation would become central to imperial Christianity, although theological conflict continued for centuries.

Constantinople was designed to rival Rome. It possessed a monumental forum, an imperial palace, public baths, churches, and a ceremonial avenue. Its location on a peninsula made it defensible, and its walls were repeatedly strengthened. The city’s natural harbor, the Golden Horn, supported trade and naval activity. Over time, Constantinople became not merely an administrative center but the symbolic heart of the eastern Roman world.

## The Division of the Roman Empire

After Constantine’s death in 337, the empire continued to be governed by members of his dynasty, but internal rivalry and external pressure remained persistent. The Roman world was never neatly divided into two entirely separate states. Emperors continued to claim authority over the whole empire, and the eastern and western halves remained connected through law, military structures, commerce, and dynastic politics.

Nevertheless, administrative separation became more pronounced. In 395, after the death of Theodosius I, the empire was again divided between his sons: Arcadius governed the East and Honorius the West. This division proved enduring in practice. The eastern empire was wealthier, more urbanized, and better able to sustain taxation and military administration. The western empire faced severe pressures from Germanic migrations, civil conflict, fiscal weakness, and the loss of territories.

The sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 shocked the Roman world. Rome remained symbolically important, but it was no longer the secure center of imperial power. In 476, the Germanic military leader Odoacer deposed the western emperor Romulus Augustulus. Traditionally, this event is treated as the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Yet the eastern emperor in Constantinople did not regard the Roman Empire as having ended. From the eastern perspective, there was still one Roman emperor, and the western territories had simply fallen under the rule of local kings and military leaders.

The eastern empire inherited Roman institutions and law, but it also developed its own character. Greek was widely spoken in the eastern provinces and eventually became the dominant language of government and culture, though Latin remained important in administration and legal tradition for centuries. Christianity provided a shared ideological framework, while the eastern Mediterranean’s cities, trade networks, and intellectual traditions sustained a vibrant urban civilization.

## Justinian and the Ambition to Restore Rome

The sixth century opened with the reign of Justinian I, one of the most consequential emperors in Roman and Byzantine history. Justinian came to power in 527 and ruled until 565. His reign combined legal reform, military reconquest, architectural magnificence, religious controversy, and political upheaval.

Justinian’s greatest legal achievement was the compilation of Roman law. Under the direction of the jurist Tribonian, imperial legislation and earlier legal writings were organized into what later generations called the Corpus Juris Civilis, or Body of Civil Law. It included the Codex, containing imperial laws; the Digest, drawn from the writings of earlier jurists; the Institutes, a textbook for legal students; and later legislation known as the Novellae. Although the compilation did not instantly replace every local legal practice, it became one of the most influential legal works in European history. Centuries later, it would shape the legal systems of much of continental Europe.

Justinian also pursued the reconquest of former western Roman territories. The general Belisarius invaded the Vandal kingdom in North Africa in 533. The campaign succeeded with surprising speed, restoring imperial control over Carthage and much of the former Vandal realm. Belisarius then turned toward Italy, where the Ostrogothic kingdom had ruled since the late fifth century. The Gothic War, beginning in 535, lasted for decades and devastated the Italian peninsula. Rome changed hands repeatedly, cities were besieged, and agricultural production suffered. By the early 550s, imperial forces had defeated the Ostrogoths, and Italy was nominally restored to Roman rule.

The empire also recovered parts of southeastern Spain from the Visigoths. Justinian’s ambition was not merely territorial. He aimed to restore the Roman imperial order around the Mediterranean. Yet reconquest was expensive, and the restored territories were vulnerable. The Lombards invaded Italy soon after Justinian’s death, limiting imperial control largely to coastal and southern regions.

Justinian’s reign is also remembered for the construction of Hagia Sophia. The previous church on the site had been destroyed during the Nika revolt of 532, a violent uprising that nearly toppled the emperor. Justinian commissioned the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus to create a vast new church. Completed in 537, Hagia Sophia’s enormous dome seemed to float above the interior, supported by an innovative system of arches and pendentives. It became the most celebrated monument of Constantinople and a symbol of imperial Christianity.

The Nika revolt revealed the volatility of urban politics. Chariot-racing factions, often associated with the Blues and Greens, had social and political significance beyond sport. Their supporters could mobilize large crowds, and tensions over taxation, legal disputes, and imperial administration contributed to the uprising. Justinian initially considered fleeing, but Empress Theodora reportedly urged him to remain and confront the crisis. The revolt was suppressed with great violence, and the rebuilding of Constantinople transformed the city.

Theodora herself was an influential political partner. She supported religious positions associated with non-Chalcedonian Christians and advocated measures affecting women’s legal and social status. Though the surviving sources reflect the prejudices of their authors, her role demonstrates that imperial power was not exercised by emperors alone.

Justinian’s policies imposed significant burdens. His wars, construction projects, and administrative apparatus required heavy taxation. The empire was also struck by plague beginning in 541, probably part of the first major pandemic historically associated with bubonic plague. The disease affected Constantinople and many other regions, reducing populations and weakening economic and military capacity. By the end of Justinian’s reign, the empire remained formidable but was strained by the cost of universal ambition.

## Crisis and Survival in the Seventh Century

The decades after Justinian were marked by instability. The empire confronted the Avars and Slavs in the Balkans, the Persian Sasanian Empire in the east, and internal political conflict. Under Emperor Heraclius, who came to power in 610, the Persian war reached an extraordinary level of intensity.

The Sasanian ruler Khosrow II seized Byzantine territories in Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and Anatolia. Persian forces captured Jerusalem in 614 and took the relic believed to be the True Cross. Egypt, a crucial source of grain and tax revenue, was lost. Constantinople itself appeared threatened.

Heraclius reorganized imperial finances and military operations. From 622 onward, he conducted a series of campaigns that shifted the balance. Byzantine forces invaded Persian territory, and in 627 defeated the Persians near Nineveh. Internal conflict within the Sasanian state led to Khosrow’s overthrow and a peace settlement. Byzantine rule was restored in much of the lost territory, but the victory was short-lived.

Within a few years, Arab armies emerging from the Arabian Peninsula conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and much of the eastern provinces. These conquests were driven by a combination of religious, political, and military factors. The Byzantine and Persian empires had exhausted one another in their long war, leaving both vulnerable. By the 640s, the eastern Mediterranean political order had been fundamentally transformed.

The loss of Egypt and Syria was a watershed. These provinces had been among the richest and most urbanized parts of the Roman world. Their loss reduced the empire’s tax base and changed its strategic priorities. The empire increasingly centered on Anatolia, Thrace, the Aegean, and Constantinople. The old Mediterranean empire became a more compact and militarized state.

Constantinople survived repeated Arab sieges, especially in 674–678 and 717–718. The city’s fortifications, naval power, and defensive technologies were crucial. Greek fire, a combustible substance used in naval warfare, was particularly feared, though its precise composition remains unknown. The survival of Constantinople prevented the eastern Roman state from suffering the fate of many neighboring powers and preserved a Christian imperial center for centuries.

The seventh century also saw profound administrative changes. The empire’s military provinces, often called themes, developed as a response to the new strategic environment. Armies were settled in regions where they could defend local territory, and military and civil administration became more closely connected. The precise origins and development of the theme system remain debated, but it helped the empire mobilize resources in a period of contraction.

The language and identity of the empire changed as well. Latin receded, while Greek became increasingly dominant in administration and public culture. Yet the rulers and inhabitants continued to identify themselves as Romans. “Roman” became a political and religious identity rather than simply a reflection of Latin language or control over the ancient city of Rome.

## Iconoclasm and the Transformation of Imperial Christianity

One of the most divisive episodes in Byzantine history was the controversy over religious images, known as Iconoclasm. Beginning in the eighth century and recurring into the ninth, emperors and churchmen argued over whether icons—painted or sculpted representations of Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the saints—were legitimate objects of devotion or a form of idolatry.

Emperor Leo III initiated policies against images in the 720s, though the exact sequence and extent of early iconoclastic measures remain debated. His son Constantine V strongly supported the movement and convened the Council of Hieria in 754, which rejected the veneration of icons. Iconoclast emperors argued that divine nature could not be represented and that the use of images blurred the distinction between Creator and creation.

Iconophile opponents defended icons as expressions of the Christian doctrine of the Incarnation. Since God had become human in Christ, they argued, the visible representation of Christ was possible and the veneration shown to an image could pass to the person represented. The theologian John of Damascus, writing under Muslim rule, became one of the most influential defenders of images.

The controversy had political dimensions. Emperors sought authority over religious institutions, monasteries, and ecclesiastical wealth. Monks were among the strongest defenders of icons, and iconoclast policies sometimes targeted monastic property and influence. The debate also affected relations with the papacy, which generally favored the veneration of images.

Iconoclasm ended decisively in 843 under Empress Theodora, who restored the veneration of icons. The event is commemorated in Eastern Orthodox Christianity as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. The controversy left a lasting mark on Byzantine theology, art, and the relationship between imperial power and the church.

## The Macedonian Renaissance

The ninth through eleventh centuries witnessed a major revival of Byzantine political power and cultural production. This era is often associated with the Macedonian dynasty, which ruled from 867 to 1056, though the term “Macedonian Renaissance” refers more broadly to intellectual and artistic renewal.

Byzantine scholars collected, copied, and commented on ancient Greek texts. Classical literature, philosophy, medicine, and science were preserved in manuscript traditions that later became crucial to the transmission of Greek learning. This was not simple imitation of antiquity. Byzantine intellectuals interpreted classical works through Christian frameworks and applied them to contemporary education, theology, and administration.

The empire’s foreign relations also expanded. Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius developed a written script and translated Christian texts for Slavic peoples. Their mission to Moravia had lasting effects, and their disciples helped spread Christianity and literacy among the Bulgarians and other Slavic communities. The script associated with their tradition, Cyrillic, became central to the written cultures of several eastern European societies.

Christianization strengthened Byzantine influence but also created new political relationships. The conversion of Bulgaria to Christianity in the ninth century was a major achievement, though relations between Byzantium and Bulgaria were often marked by warfare. The Bulgarian ruler Simeon I sought recognition as emperor and challenged Constantinople militarily and diplomatically. The conflict ended only after prolonged struggle.

Under Basil II, who ruled from 976 to 1025, the empire reached a high point. Basil is remembered in later tradition as the “Bulgar-Slayer,” a title reflecting his campaigns against the Bulgarian Empire. Byzantine forces defeated Bulgaria after decades of war, and the region was incorporated into the imperial sphere. Basil also strengthened control in Armenia and expanded influence in the Caucasus.

The military and administrative structures of the middle Byzantine period were sophisticated. Provincial commanders, aristocratic landowners, and military families competed for influence. The state sought to preserve the tax base and prevent powerful magnates from absorbing the land of small farmers. Laws attempted to limit the concentration of land, though enforcement varied.

The imperial court in Constantinople became a center of ceremonial, diplomacy, and political theater. Foreign ambassadors were impressed—or intimidated—by elaborate rituals designed to present the emperor as the earthly representative of divine order. Byzantine diplomacy relied not only on military force but also on marriage alliances, gifts, titles, religious missions, intelligence gathering, and the manipulation of rival powers.

## The Great Schism and Relations with the Latin West

Relations between the Byzantine church and the Latin church had long been marked by differences in language, liturgy, ecclesiastical organization, and political culture. These tensions eventually contributed to the schism traditionally dated to 1054.

The dispute involved papal authority, the jurisdiction of the patriarch of Constantinople, liturgical customs, and theological differences such as the Filioque controversy. Western Christians increasingly included the phrase “and the Son” in the creed’s statement about the procession of the Holy Spirit. Byzantine theologians objected both to the theological formulation and to the unilateral alteration of the creed.

In 1054, representatives of Pope Leo IX and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchanged excommunications. The event was not immediately understood as an irreversible division across all Christian communities, and communication continued afterward. Yet it came to symbolize the growing separation between Roman Catholicism in the West and Eastern Orthodoxy in the Byzantine world.

The schism should not be reduced to a single moment. Centuries of institutional and cultural divergence lay behind it, and later events deepened the rupture. The relationship between Byzantium and western Europe was shaped by mutual admiration, suspicion, competition, and misunderstanding.

## The Crisis of the Eleventh Century

After Basil II’s death, the empire faced growing political instability. Civil wars, succession disputes, fiscal problems, and pressure from external enemies weakened central authority. The arrival of the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia created a new and formidable challenge.

At the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes was defeated and captured by the Seljuk ruler Alp Arslan. The battle itself did not instantly destroy Byzantine power, and its strategic consequences were complicated by civil war. But the subsequent political disorder enabled Turkish forces to establish themselves across much of Anatolia, the empire’s principal recruiting ground and economic heartland.

Anatolia had been central to Byzantine survival since the seventh century. Its loss reduced manpower, tax revenue, and agricultural production. The empire’s military system was increasingly dependent on foreign mercenaries, and provincial elites gained leverage over imperial politics.

The emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who came to power in 1081, stabilized the state through a combination of military reform, diplomacy, and fiscal measures. He faced Normans in the Balkans, Pechenegs north of the Danube, and Turkish powers in Anatolia. Alexios appealed to the papacy and western rulers for military assistance, contributing to the launching of the First Crusade.

The crusading movement created both opportunity and danger. Western armies passed through Byzantine territory, and Alexios hoped they would help recover lands lost to the Turks. He sought oaths from crusader leaders promising to return former imperial territories. Some cooperation occurred, and Nicaea was restored to Byzantine control. But mutual distrust soon grew. Latin leaders established their own principalities in the Levant, and Byzantine-western relations deteriorated.

The Komnenian emperors maintained a reduced but influential empire. Alexios, John II, and Manuel I strengthened the army, cultivated aristocratic networks, and projected power into the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. Manuel I in particular pursued an ambitious foreign policy involving Hungary, Italy, the Crusader states, and the Muslim powers of the Near East.

Yet the restoration was fragile. The empire’s dependence on aristocratic families and foreign military forces created structural weaknesses. Commercial privileges granted to Italian maritime republics brought short-term benefits but gradually undermined Byzantine control of trade.

## The Fourth Crusade and the Sack of Constantinople

The catastrophe of 1204 was one of the most consequential events in Byzantine history. The Fourth Crusade, initially intended to attack Muslim Egypt, became entangled in Venetian financial interests and Byzantine dynastic politics.

The crusaders agreed to assist the deposed Byzantine prince Alexios Angelos, who promised money, military support, and church union in exchange for help restoring his father to the throne. After entering Constantinople in 1203, the crusaders restored Isaac II and Alexios IV. Their promises proved impossible to fulfill, and resentment between the local population and the western forces intensified.

In April 1204, crusader armies captured and sacked Constantinople. Churches, palaces, libraries, and private homes were looted. The violence shocked contemporaries, including some western Christian observers. The Hagia Sophia was desecrated, relics were carried away, and the city’s wealth was dispersed across Europe.

The crusaders established the Latin Empire of Constantinople. Byzantine territories were divided among Latin rulers, Venetian interests, and local Greek successor states. The principal Byzantine centers of resistance were the Empire of Nicaea in western Anatolia, the Despotate of Epirus in the Balkans, and the Empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea coast.

The Empire of Nicaea eventually emerged as the strongest successor state. Its rulers preserved imperial institutions, supported the Orthodox church, and gradually recovered territory. In 1261, Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured Constantinople and restored Byzantine rule.

The empire that returned to Constantinople was greatly diminished. The city’s population had fallen, its economy was damaged, and much of the former imperial territory was controlled by rival states. The restored empire had to contend with Venice, Genoa, western principalities, Balkan rulers, and Turkish powers.

The sack of 1204 permanently damaged relations between Byzantium and the Latin West. Although negotiations over church union continued, many Byzantines regarded western military and religious ambitions as more dangerous than any temporary alliance might be useful.

## The Palaiologan Era

The Palaiologan dynasty ruled from 1259 until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Its reign was characterized by cultural brilliance, political fragmentation, military weakness, and eventual Ottoman conquest.

Michael VIII Palaiologos sought to secure the restored empire diplomatically. At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, he accepted a form of church union with Rome in hopes of preventing a western attack. The agreement faced strong opposition among Byzantine clergy and population. Many Byzantines believed that doctrinal compromise threatened Orthodox identity, while the promised military assistance was limited.

The union failed to produce lasting security. Byzantine resources were stretched by conflicts in the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Mediterranean. Genoa and Venice competed for commercial privileges, and the empire increasingly relied on foreign powers whose interests did not align with Constantinople’s.

Under Andronikos II, the empire’s military capacity declined. The reduction of the navy and reliance on mercenaries weakened defenses. In Anatolia, Turkish principalities expanded rapidly. Among them was the Ottoman polity, founded by Osman in the late thirteenth century. The Ottomans initially controlled territory in northwestern Anatolia but soon crossed into Europe and established themselves in the Balkans.

The fourteenth century brought civil wars, financial crises, plague, and territorial losses. The empire became a patchwork of Constantinople, parts of the Peloponnese, Thessaloniki at various times, and scattered holdings. The Ottoman advance was relentless, though Byzantine diplomacy sometimes exploited rivalries among Ottoman princes and neighboring states.

The Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347 was especially destructive. Competing factions supported different candidates for the throne, and foreign powers intervened. The conflict weakened the state and enabled Ottoman expansion. The empire’s remaining resources were further diminished by the Black Death, which reached Constantinople and other regions in the mid-fourteenth century.

Despite political decline, the Palaiologan period was a time of remarkable intellectual and artistic achievement. Byzantine scholars studied ancient philosophy and science, and some later traveled to Italy, contributing to the Renaissance’s renewed interest in Greek learning. Manuscript production continued, as did theological debate and artistic innovation.

The hesychast controversy, associated with Gregory Palamas, concerned the nature of mystical prayer and the possibility of experiencing divine grace. Palamas distinguished between God’s inaccessible essence and the divine energies through which God could be experienced. The controversy reflected the continuing vitality of Byzantine theology even amid political crisis.

The empire’s cultural influence extended beyond its borders. Orthodox Christianity shaped the religious and political traditions of Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, and other eastern European societies. Byzantine artistic forms, liturgical practices, legal ideas, and models of rulership continued to influence neighboring civilizations long after imperial territory had contracted.

## The Final Struggle

By the fifteenth century, Constantinople was largely surrounded by Ottoman lands. The city remained symbolically powerful and possessed formidable walls, but its population and economic base had greatly declined. The Byzantine emperors appealed repeatedly to western Europe for assistance, often linking aid to church union.

Emperor John VIII Palaiologos attended the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438–1439. A union between the Greek and Latin churches was proclaimed, but it was unpopular among many Byzantines and did not generate sufficient military support. The slogan that it was better to see the Turkish turban in Constantinople than the Latin mitre captured the depth of opposition to western ecclesiastical control, though its exact historical context is debated.

In 1451, Mehmed II became Ottoman sultan. He was determined to capture Constantinople and transform it into the center of a new imperial order. He constructed the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the European shore of the Bosporus, strengthened Ottoman artillery, and assembled a large army.

The siege began in April 1453. Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos commanded a small defending force composed of Byzantines, Genoese, Venetians, and other volunteers. The city’s walls remained formidable, but the defenders were vastly outnumbered. Ottoman cannon battered the fortifications, while ships attempted to blockade the harbor. Mehmed famously transported ships overland into the Golden Horn to bypass the defensive chain.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottomans launched their final assault. Constantine XI disappeared in the fighting and was remembered as a heroic final emperor. Constantinople fell, ending the Byzantine Empire after more than a thousand years of imperial history.

The conquest was not the end of the city. Mehmed II made Constantinople—soon increasingly called Istanbul—the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The city was repopulated and rebuilt, while Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque. Byzantine administrative, artistic, and intellectual traditions continued within the Ottoman world.

## Legacy

The Byzantine Empire’s legacy is vast and complex. It preserved Roman law, statecraft, Christianity, and Greek learning through centuries when political structures in the western Mediterranean were transformed. Its scholars copied ancient texts that might otherwise have been lost. Its theologians shaped Eastern Orthodox Christianity. Its artists developed the icon, mosaic, manuscript illumination, and architectural traditions that influenced regions from the Balkans to Russia.

Its political culture also left a deep imprint. The Byzantine emperor was portrayed as God’s chosen ruler and guardian of Christian order, though emperors were frequently challenged, deposed, or killed. The empire’s diplomacy anticipated forms of international politics based on ceremonial status, dynastic marriage, intelligence, subsidies, and indirect influence.

Byzantium’s history also demonstrates the adaptability of imperial systems. It survived the collapse of the western Roman world, the rise of Islam, the loss of major provinces, religious civil conflict, and the devastation of 1204. It repeatedly reorganized its institutions and redefined its identity while maintaining a continuous claim to Roman legitimacy.

At the same time, its decline was not caused by a single weakness. It resulted from overlapping pressures: shrinking territory, fiscal strain, aristocratic rivalry, military dependence, commercial concessions, epidemic disease, civil war, and the rise of powerful external states. The Fourth Crusade inflicted a wound from which the empire never fully recovered, while the Ottoman conquest completed a transformation already underway.

To study Byzantium is therefore to study continuity amid change. The empire was Roman in its political memory, Greek in much of its language and culture, Christian in its worldview, and profoundly shaped by the peoples and powers around it. Its thousand-year history cannot be reduced either to a fading remnant of Rome or to a separate civilization disconnected from antiquity. It was a living, evolving society that carried the Roman imperial tradition into the medieval world—and whose influence remains visible in law, religion, art, architecture, literature, and political thought today.
